newsitem.title: UK: LME RE-ITERATES CONCERNS OVER MARKET ABUSE.
newsitem.headline: LME RE-ITERATES CONCERNS OVER MARKET ABUSE.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME), in a notice to members, has drawn attention to rules regarding market conditions and abuse.

In the notice LME Chief Executive David King highlighted member obligations under its own rules, as well as principles laid down by the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) in its review of the metals market.
Certain LME rules refer to trading purposes, and are particularly relevant in relation to criminal offences set out in section 47 of the Financial Services Act (FSA).
"...the (LME) Board underlines the fact that, even without having had any untoward intent, a member may find that it has come to exercise a dominant position in the market," it said.
Circumstances may vary, but a member could have a long position which is large in relation to the stock available for delivery.

"The dominance of its position may mean that in order to ensure that its trades are proper, to avoid the creation of a disorderly market or other undesirable situation, and to ensure that the market is not brought into disrepute it has to act with particular caution," the LME said.
When assessing such issues, the LME Board or disciplinary committee may judge the effect on market conditions, whether or not the parties involved intended to create such conditions, it added.
The LME also noted SIB principles, in particular on occasions where the LME limits the daily backwardation on certain contracts.
The limit is for the market's protection, but cannot provide guidance on what is a proper trade or acceptable conduct.
"It was possible that the limit on the backwardation could be reached in tight market conditions where all buyers and sellers were trading properly and none was in a dominant position."
However, using a dominant position to force other market users to pay more than they would motherwise had to pay is improper, even if the price is below the backwardation limit, it added.
On the LME three of its markets are currently in backwardation, reflecting tightness, giving concern over possible squeezes.

Copper holds a $30 backwardation at present, but the cash/threes premium was over $300 at one stage this year. The LME currently has a limit on the daily backwardation equal to one percent of the previous day's cash settlement. This limit has been hit on occasions this year.
More recently, tightness has developed in aluminium and zinc. Aluminium has a cash/threes backwardation of $13/16, while the zinc premium is around $100.
The LME said that its notice was for guidance - it has not changed any rules, but is summarising their effect.
"In the event of a breach of the LME rules, the LME will not hesitate to take disciplinary proceedings against members," the LME said.
